relations.note: Ninsun is consistently Gilgamesh’s mother in the mature literary tradition.
relations.source: Old Babylonian epic; Standard Babylonian Tablets I–III

relations.myth: Ninsun interprets dreams and intercedes for the expedition
relations.note: She interprets Gilgamesh’s dreams and petitions Šamaš to protect him.
The dominant later genealogy makes the deified Lugalbanda Gilgamesh’s father.
relations.source: God lists and Babylonian epic genealogy

relations.note: Some King List manuscripts name a lillû as Gilgamesh’s father.
The Sumerian Bull composition calls Peštur Gilgamesh’s little sister.
relations.source: Gilgamesh and the Bull of Heaven

relations.note: At Anu’s command, Aruru creates Enkidu as Gilgamesh’s equal and check.
Enkidu blocks Gilgamesh, and the two wrestle before becoming companions.
relations.source: Old Babylonian and Standard Babylonian epic

relations.note: The companions journey together and defeat and kill Humbaba.
Gilgamesh and Enkidu jointly kill the divine Bull attacking Uruk.
relations.source: Sumerian Bull; Standard Babylonian Tablet VI

relations.myth: Enkidu descends for the pukku and mēkku
relations.note: Enkidu volunteers as Gilgamesh’s servant to retrieve objects from the netherworld.
Enkidu’s death causes Gilgamesh’s grief and quest against mortality.
Learned god lists pair Gilgamesh and Enkidu as underworld-related divine figures.
Gilgamesh offers deceptive gifts or marriages to strip Huwawa’s protections.

relations.myth: Defeat of the Cedar Forest guardian
relations.note: Gilgamesh kills Humbaba with Enkidu despite the guardian’s plea for mercy.
Šamaš authorizes the expedition and sends winds that immobilize Humbaba.
Šamaš argues in favor of Gilgamesh and Enkidu before the gods.
At Enki’s command, Utu opens a fissure and returns Enkidu’s shade.
Enlil responds angrily to Humbaba’s killing and redistributes the guardian’s auras.

relations.myth: Divine council after the Bull’s death
relations.note: Enlil supports the judgment that one of the two heroes must die.
Gilgamesh appeals to Enlil, who does not release Enkidu from below.
Gilgamesh appeals to Suen, who does not grant Enkidu’s release.
Enki answers Gilgamesh’s appeal and orders Utu to release Enkidu’s shade.
Gilgamesh expels its occupants, cuts the tree, and fashions implements for Inana.

relations.myth: Conflict over the Bull of Heaven
relations.note: Inana releases the Bull against Uruk; Gilgamesh kills it and insults her.
relations.source: Gilgamesh and the Bull of Heaven

relations.note: Gilgamesh rejects Ištar’s sexual or marital proposal and recounts her lovers’ fates.
Gilgamesh and Enkidu battle the divine Bull released against Uruk.
relations.source: Sumerian Bull; Standard Babylonian Tablet VI

relations.note: Gilgamesh and Enkidu kill the Bull after it devastates Uruk.
relations.source: Sumerian Bull; Standard Babylonian Tablet VI

relations.myth: Release of the Bull of Heaven
relations.note: An gives Inana the Bull whose attack brings Gilgamesh into conflict.
relations.source: Sumerian Bull; Standard Babylonian Tablet VI

relations.myth: Divine council after the Bull’s death
relations.note: Anu joins the council judging the heroes and deciding Enkidu must die.

relations.myth: Ninsun’s prayer for the Cedar expedition
relations.note: Aya participates indirectly when Ninsun petitions Šamaš and his wife.

relations.myth: Flood account and lesson on mortality
relations.note: The immortal flood survivor recounts the flood and explains mortality to Gilgamesh.
relations.source: Old Babylonian antecedents; Standard Tablets X–XI

relations.note: Uta-napišti tests Gilgamesh, who fails to remain awake.
Uta-napišti tells Gilgamesh where to obtain the youth-renewing plant.
A snake steals Gilgamesh’s plant while he bathes and sheds its skin.
Siduri counsels Gilgamesh during his search for the immortal flood survivor.
relations.source: Old Babylonian Sippar; Standard Tablet X

relations.note: Ur-šanabi ferries Gilgamesh across the Waters of Death to Uta-napišti.

relations.myth: Passage through the mountains of Māšu
relations.note: Gilgamesh encounters the scorpion-beings while seeking the road beyond Māšu.
Gilgamesh drives the Anzud bird from Inana’s occupied tree.
Gilgamesh exercises judicial office within the underworld realm ruled by Ereškigal.
Later theology places Gilgamesh’s judicial office within Nergal’s underworld administration.
Gilgamesh and Dumuzi share chthonic offering contexts without secure direct dialogue.
Gilgamesh and Ningishzida appear together among underworld powers and offerings.
The underworld scribe shares the Tablet XII setting with Gilgamesh.
